a_cooking.thesis: Cooking is the centre: every other application here (balm, lotion, diffuser, candle) reuses the same three facts learned at the stove - aroma molecules are mostly fat-soluble and volatile, heat both releases and destroys them, and water plus low oxygen plus low acid is where food-poisoning organisms live.

solubility.principle: Most aroma and pungency compounds are terpenes, phenylpropanoids, or alkaloid/amides with low water solubility (log P roughly 2-5). Fat and ethanol extract them; water extracts sugars, acids, glycosides, tannins, pigments like crocin and anthocyanins.

table.practical: Milk/yoghurt/fat relieve burn better than water; chilli oil (la you) and tadka carry heat through a dish.
Bloom cracked pepper in fat; pepper added late tastes sharper (volatile terpenes) than pepper cooked long.

table.water: practically insoluble at neutral pH; degrades fast above pH 7
table.practical: Fry turmeric in oil; yellow turns red-brown in alkali (baking soda) - a pH indicator.

Formed only when cell is crushed WITH water (myrosinase on sinigrin). Mix mustard powder with COLD water, wait 10 min, then add acid/heat; heat or vinegar first kills the enzyme and the bite. Black mustard seeds popped in hot oil are nutty, not hot.

table.fat: decomposes to ajoenes/diallyl sulfides in oil
table.practical: Crush and rest 10 min before heating to let alliinase work; heat-killed garlic is sweet, not sharp.
Steep saffron in warm water or milk, not oil (safranal aroma is the volatile, fat-friendly part).
Acid keeps them red; alkali turns blue/green.
Why vanilla extract is a 35%+ ethanol extract (US 21 CFR 169.175 - "not less than 35 percent ethyl alcohol"; unverified this session).

solubility.status: logP values approximate (PubChem XLogP3 range); qualitative solubility from standard references - secondary
solubility.our_page_claim: Cooking_with_Herbs_and_Spices cites a "lab test" with ~10x thymol in oil vs water. Directionally right (partition), but the specific test is a popular-press (test-kitchen) experiment, not a citable study - flagged unverified.

blooming_tadka.what: Whole or ground spices fried briefly in hot fat (ghee, mustard oil, sesame oil) - tadka/tarka/chaunk/baghaar (South Asia), also the Sichuan hot-oil pour, Mexican toasted-chile salsas.
why: Dissolves fat-soluble aroma into the fat so it coats every mouthful
Hot fat (160-190 C) drives Maillard and caramelisation on seed surfaces and pyrolysis-like roast notes
Pops mustard seeds (steam explosion) and releases cumin/fennel terpenoids
Finishes a dal or raita by pouring sizzling oil over at the end: aroma arrives at the table un-boiled
blooming_tadka.order: Seeds that tolerate heat first (mustard until it pops, cumin until it darkens a shade, 10-30 s), then dried chillies and curry leaves (splatter), then asafoetida for 2-3 s, then ground spices for seconds only, then liquid or pour over. Asafoetida and ground turmeric/chilli burn in seconds.

heat_timing.principle: Monoterpenes (limonene bp 176 C, linalool 198 C, 1,8-cineole 176 C) steam-distil out of a simmering pot even below their boiling points because they co-distil with water vapour (steam distillation is exactly how essential oils are made). Sesquiterpenes and phenylpropanoids (beta-caryophyllene, eugenol bp 254 C) and non-volatile pungents (capsaicin, piperine) persist.
rules: Hardy/woody herbs and whole seed spices early; leafy herbs, citrus zest, and fresh chilli/garlic aroma late or raw
Lid on keeps volatiles in a braise; lid off reduces and loses them
Split additions: half early for depth, half at the end for top notes
Long-cooked garlic and onion lose sulfur bite and gain sweetness (thermal breakdown + Maillard)
heat_timing.status: boiling points from standard tables (unverified this session); principle textbook

toasting_maillard.chemistry: Maillard reaction = reducing sugars + amino acids/peptides above roughly 120-140 C at low water activity; produces pyrazines (roasty, nutty), furans, thiazoles, Strecker aldehydes. Caramelisation (sugars alone) needs ~160 C+ for sucrose. Dry-toasting seeds removes surface water so the surface can pass 100 C.
toasting_maillard.acrylamide: Asparagine + reducing sugar at high temperature forms acrylamide (EU Regulation 2017/2158 benchmark levels; "go for gold" - brown, not dark). Toast spices and bread to golden, not black.
toasting_maillard.alkaline_trick: A pinch of baking soda raises pH and speeds Maillard (caramelised onions, pretzels, ramen kansui) - and ruins anthocyanin colour and some vitamins.
toasting_maillard.status: textbook chemistry; acrylamide regulation cited from memory (unverified)

Tenderise surfaces (ceviche denatures protein, does not reliably kill parasites/bacteria)
Fix colours: anthocyanins red; chlorophyll turns olive-drab in acid during cooking - add acid to green vegetables at the end

antimicrobial_evidence.source: Billing J, Sherman PW. Antimicrobial functions of spices: why some like it hot. Q Rev Biol 1998;73(1):3-49.
key_points: Analysed traditional meat-based recipes from many countries; spice use rises with mean annual temperature (hotter climates, faster spoilage, more spices, more potent antibacterials)
Garlic, onion, allspice and oregano were the most broadly inhibitory of the spices reviewed (reported to inhibit essentially all bacteria tested)
Lemon/lime juice synergise; black pepper is weak on its own but common
Interpretation is contested (alternative: spices mask spoilage, or correlate with plant diversity and poverty) - correlation, not proof
Practical: spices are NOT a substitute for refrigeration, acidification or cooking. Concentrations in food are often below lab MICs.
antimicrobial_evidence.companion: Sherman PW, Hash GA 2001 Evol Hum Behav "Why vegetable recipes are not very spicy" (vegetables spoil less, are less spiced).
antimicrobial_evidence.study_scale: 4,578 meat-based recipes from 93 cookbooks, 36 countries, 43 spices
antimicrobial_evidence.finding: As mean annual temperature rose, the proportion of recipes with spices, spices per recipe, total spices used and use of the most potent antibacterial spices all increased; estimated fraction of bacterial species inhibited per recipe correlated with temperature.

potency_tiers_press_release.garlic, onion, allspice, oregano: inhibited every species in the compiled lab data ("kill everything")

pairing_theory.source: Ahn YY, Ahnert SE, Bagrow JP, Barabasi AL. Flavor network and the principles of food pairing. Sci Rep 2011;1:196.
key_points: Built a network of ingredients linked by shared flavour compounds from ~56,000 online recipes
North American and Western European cuisines tend to combine ingredients that share many compounds (the "food pairing hypothesis" holds there)
East Asian cuisines (Korean, Chinese, Japanese) tend to AVOID compound-sharing pairs - the hypothesis is cuisine-specific, not universal
A few ingredients (milk, butter, eggs, cocoa in the West; soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger, garlic in East Asia) dominate each cuisine's signature
Follow-up: Jain, Rakhi, Bagler 2015 (Sci Rep / PLoS) found Indian cuisine shows strong NEGATIVE food pairing, driven by spices

regional_logic.logic: Contrasting (non-shared) spices layered in fat: tadka; garam masala late; souring with tamarind, amchur, kokum, yoghurt
Contrast and fermentation umami (soy, miso, doenjang, fish sauce); aromatics garlic-ginger-scallion; sesame oil finish
Olive oil + acid + herbs; sumac, za'atar, mint, parsley; spice blends baharat, ras el hanout
Red palm oil, chilli, smoked fish, fermented locust bean (dawadawa/iru), grains of paradise, uziza
Toasted then rehydrated dried chillies, nixtamalised corn, epazote, achiote, Mexican oregano, chocolate in mole
Dairy fat, dill, caraway, juniper, mustard, horseradish; salt/smoke/ferment preservation

pairing_theory.study_scale: 56,498 recipes (epicurious, allrecipes, menupan.com), 381 ingredients, 1,021 flavour compounds, five regional cuisines

infusions.safety_core: C. botulinum spores are on garlic, herbs, vegetables and in soil. Oil excludes oxygen; garlic/fresh herbs supply moisture and are low-acid (garlic pH ~5.3-6.3). At room temperature that is an anaerobic, low-acid, moist niche where spores germinate and make toxin without obvious spoilage. Refrigeration (<= 3.3 C / 38 F stops non-proteolytic type E/B; type A proteolytic needs ~10 C+) and acid (pH <= 4.6) are the controls.

rules.product: Fresh garlic, fresh herbs or vegetables in oil, unacidified (home)
rules.rule: Refrigerate at once and use within 4 days, or freeze. Never store at room temperature. Dried garlic/herbs in oil are treated the same way by OSU (refrigerate, 4 days, or freeze).
rules.source: Oregon State Univ. Extension SP 50-701 (rev. 2025); PNW 664 (Univ. Idaho/OSU/WSU): "refrigeration for a maximum of 2 to 4 days or freezing"

rules.product: Acidified garlic/basil/oregano/rosemary in oil (tested home method)
rules.rule: Soak in 3% citric acid (1 tablespoon citric acid in 2 cups water) for 24 h at room temperature: garlic 1 part chopped (pieces <= 1/4 inch) to 3 parts solution by weight; basil/oregano/rosemary 1 part fresh herb to 10 parts solution. Drain, cover with oil. Lemon juice, vinegar and ascorbic acid are NOT tested substitutes; weaker solutions or shorter soaks can be unsafe. Refrigeration then recommended for quality, not required for safety.

After the Feb 1989 Kingston NY outbreak FDA required microbial inhibitors or acidifying agents (phosphoric/citric acid) in shelf-stable garlic-in-oil, and "Requires Refrigeration" labelling for the rest; FDA consumer bulletin 1993 warned against homemade spices-in-oil.
rules.source: Morse et al. 1990; Nummer et al. 2011 Food Prot Trends 31(6):336-342

rules.rule: Vancouver 1985: type B botulism, ~34-37 cases from a restaurant's commercial chopped garlic in soybean oil left unrefrigerated for months (St Louis 1988). Kingston NY 1989: 3 cases, garlic bread made with garlic-in-oil; leftover pH 5.7 with toxin (Morse 1990).

rules.product: Dried herbs / dried spices in oil (cosmetic or culinary)
rules.rule: Lower risk than fresh (low water activity), but OSU still classes dried garlic/herbs in oil with fresh for culinary storage (4 days refrigerated). Strain solids; watch rancidity.

3-4 sprigs fresh herbs or 3 tablespoons dried per pint of 5% vinegar; sterilise bottles (boil 10 min); optionally heat vinegar to 190-195 F (88-91 C); condition 3-4 weeks cool and dark; best within 4-6 months; not for pickling unless 5% acidity is maintained.
Perishable dairy: refrigerate, 1-2 weeks; freeze for months. Raw garlic in butter at room temperature = same botulism logic.

rules.product: Infused honey and fermented garlic honey
rules.rule: Use dried herbs/spices for plain infused honey. Fermented garlic honey is a low-acid-start ferment: check pH with a meter or narrow-range strips and keep below 4.6 (a fixed "tablespoon of vinegar" is not a tested method). Never give honey to infants under 12 months, including honey pacifiers (CDC; 162 lab-confirmed US infant botulism cases in 2018).
rules.status: verified (CDC); fermented-garlic-honey method unverified - no tested extension protocol found

infusions.acidification_note: Acid must penetrate the food, not just the oil (acid does not dissolve in oil). That is why tested methods soak garlic in acid before oil.
infusions.source_disagreement: Cornell Extension gives up to 10 days for refrigerated garlic-in-oil; OSU/PNW 664 give 2-4 days. Use the shorter figure.

anhydrous_ratios.note: All by WEIGHT. Anhydrous (no water) = no preservative needed, only an antioxidant to slow rancidity. Hardness depends on wax type and room temperature.

table.feel: whip when semi-set at ~ 20 C; may add 1-2% starch/arrowroot to cut grease
firm stick; the 1:1:1 oil:butter:wax by weight is a common starting point
plus 10-25% fragrance/essential oil - check dermal limits; IFRA cat 4 applies

wax_substitution.factor: use ~33-50%; much higher melt, can be brittle

wax_substitution.swap: beeswax -> sunflower or rice bran wax

wax_substitution.factor: not equivalent; soft, use more and expect a greasier set

hardness_adjustment: Spoon test: dip a cold spoon, freeze 2-5 min, test feel; add oil to soften, wax to firm, in ~2-5% steps of total
Hot climates: +2-5% wax or swap part butter for cocoa/kokum; cold climates: more liquid oil
Graininess with shea/mango/cocoa: melt fully, hold ~75-80 C 15-20 min, cool fast
Add essential oils and heat-sensitive actives (vitamin E, CO2 extracts) below ~60 C, just before pouring
anhydrous_ratios.antioxidant: Mixed tocopherols 0.1-0.5% of oil phase, or rosemary CO2 extract (carnosic acid) 0.05-0.2%. These slow rancidity only; they are NOT preservatives.

types.O/W (oil-in-water): Lotions and creams; water is the continuous phase - light, washable, needs a broad-spectrum preservative. Most modern lotions.
types.W/O (water-in-oil): Cold cream, heavy barrier creams, nappy creams; oil continuous - greasier, more occlusive, still needs preservation if water is present.

HLB.definition: Griffin (1949) hydrophile-lipophile balance, 0-20 for non-ionics: HLB = 20 x (mass of hydrophilic portion / total mass). Low HLB (3-6) favours W/O; 8-18 favours O/W.
HLB.blend_math: HLB_blend = sum(fraction_i x HLB_i). Example: to hit HLB 7 with Span 80 (4.3) and Tween 80 (15.0): x*15 + (1-x)*4.3 = 7 -> x = 0.25 Tween 80, 0.75 Span 80.
HLB.status: verified (Griffin 1949 J Soc Cosmet Chem 1(5):311-326 tables via agent)

emulsifier_choices.name: Emulsifying wax NF (cetearyl alcohol + polysorbate 60)
emulsifier_choices.typical_use: supplier rule: ~25% of the oil phase (+1%); typical 3-5% lotions, 5-10% creams (Lotioncrafter; Polawax NF 2-10%)
emulsifier_choices.notes: Forgiving workhorse; NF monograph defines composition. "Emulsifying wax" without NF can be anything.

emulsifier_choices.name: Olivem 1000 (cetearyl olivate + sorbitan olivate)
emulsifier_choices.typical_use: 1.5-4% as sole emulsifier (3-4% for higher viscosity) per Hallstar distributor; retailers say 3-5%
emulsifier_choices.notes: Needs slow cooling with gentle stirring; thin alone - pair with cetyl alcohol or a gum; skin feel "natural" claim.

emulsifier_choices.name: BTMS-25 / BTMS-50 (behentrimonium methosulfate + cetearyl alcohol [+ butylene glycol])
emulsifier_choices.typical_use: BTMS-50: 1-10% (retailer data); BTMS-25: no supplier rate found
emulsifier_choices.notes: Conditioning, powdery feel; positively charged - compatible with cationic/non-ionic only; avoid mixing with anionic gums/surfactants. "Mild" quat but still a quat for eye area.

emulsifier_choices.name: Beeswax + borax (historic cold cream)
emulsifier_choices.notes: Borax is restricted in EU cosmetics (CMR 1B; not in products for under-3s; limits) - historical interest; prefer modern emulsifiers.

emulsions.heat_and_hold: Heat the water phase and oil phase separately to ~70-75 C and HOLD the water phase there for ~20 min. The hold is a habit from industry: it lets waxes and emulsifiers fully melt/hydrate and it reduces (does NOT eliminate) microbial load; it is not sterilisation and does not replace a preservative. Weigh the water phase before and after and top up evaporated water, or the percentages drift. Combine (water into oil or oil into water per emulsifier instructions), stick-blend 1-3 min, then stir while cooling; add heat-sensitive ingredients (preservative per its max temp, fragrance, actives) at the "cool-down" phase, typically below 40-45 C.

standard_formula_template_O_W_lotion.ingredients: distilled water to 100%; glycerin 2-5%; xanthan 0.2% (pre-dispersed in glycerin)
carrier oils/butters 15-25%; emulsifier (e.g. e-wax NF 4-5% or Olivem 1000 4%); cetyl alcohol 1-2%
broad-spectrum preservative at label rate; tocopherol 0.2-0.5%; essential oil within dermal limit; pH adjust to 4.5-5.5 with citric acid / sodium hydroxide solution

preservatives.why: Any product containing free water (lotions, creams, sprays, hydrosols, aloe gels, scrubs used in a wet shower, "oil" products contaminated by wet fingers) supports bacteria, yeast and mould within days. Contamination is often invisible (Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, Candida, Aspergillus). A broad-spectrum system covers Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, yeast and mould. Anhydrous balms/oils/butters do not need one, only an antioxidant.
not_preservatives: Vitamin E (tocopherol) - antioxidant for oils, no antimicrobial action at use levels

Grapefruit seed extract - von Woedtke et al. 1999 Pharmazie (PMID 10399191) found the antimicrobial activity of commercial GSE tracked contaminating synthetic preservatives (benzethonium chloride, triclosan, methylparaben); GSE free of them was inactive. (verified) Takeoka et al. 2005 J Agric Food Chem (PMID 16159196) identified benzalkonium chloride in commercial GSEs.
Essential oils at skin-safe levels - not reliably broad-spectrum
Leucidal Liquid - manufacturer-only evidence, weak on yeast/mould; not a stand-alone preservative

examples.use_rate: 0.5-1.0% (manufacturer); max 1.11% blend keeps phenoxyethanol at the EU 1.0% Annex V limit

examples.name: Geogard ECT (benzyl alcohol 77-86%, salicylic acid 8-15%, glycerin 3-6%, sorbic acid 1-4%)
examples.pH: 3-8 per TDS (organic acids work best at the low end)
examples.note: Salicylic acid EU max 0.5% and not in products for under-3s (except shampoo)

examples.name: Sodium benzoate + potassium sorbate
examples.use_rate: benzoic acid/sodium benzoate: 2.5% rinse-off, 1.7% oral, 0.5% leave-on (as acid); sorbic acid/salts 0.6% (as acid)
examples.spectrum: yeast/mould strong, bacteria weaker - pair with a booster

examples.name: Dehydroacetic acid + benzyl alcohol (Cosgard / Geogard 221 type)
examples.use_rate: per supplier; DHA EU max 0.6% as acid, not in aerosol sprays; benzyl alcohol 1.0%
examples.status: limits verified (Annex V); use rate unverified

examples.name: Leucidal Liquid SF (Leuconostoc/radish root ferment filtrate)
examples.note: Only manufacturer challenge data found; no independent peer-reviewed validation located; even the retailer flags weak yeast/mould coverage. Do not rely on it alone.

preservatives.challenge_testing: Only a preservative efficacy test (ISO 11930 / USP <51>) proves a formula is preserved; supplier "use rate" is a starting point. Small-batch makers can buy challenge testing from contract labs.
preservatives.pH_testing: Measure pH of the finished emulsion (dilute 1:10 in distilled water if thick) with a calibrated meter (two-point calibration with pH 4 and 7 buffers); paper strips are coarse (+-0.5-1). Target skin-compatible pH 4.5-5.5 for leave-on; preservative choice must match the pH. Re-test after 24 h and after 1 month.

herb_infused_oil_method.use_dried_material: Dry herbs to brittle (<~10% moisture). Fresh plant water carries spoilage organisms and, under oil, creates the low-oxygen moist niche (botulism logic from cooking applies to oils that might be eaten or used on broken skin; for cosmetic oils the more common failure is mould/rancidity).
herb_infused_oil_method.wilt_exception: Traditional exceptions (fresh St John's wort flowers for hypericin-red oil; wilted calendula/comfrey) are made by wilting 12-24 h first and decanting off the water layer; higher spoilage risk.
herb_infused_oil_method.ratio: 1:5 to 1:10 dried herb : oil by weight (or loosely pack jar 1/2-3/4 with dried herb, cover by 2-3 cm oil).
herb_infused_oil_method.warm: Double boiler / water bath / slow-cooker "warm" at 40-60 C for 2-8 h (up to 24-72 h at ~40 C). Keep below 60-70 C for volatile-rich herbs. Never deep-fry.
herb_infused_oil_method.cold_solar: 2-6 weeks in a sealed jar, out of direct sun (heat cycling + UV oxidise oil), shake daily.
herb_infused_oil_method.finish: Strain, press, settle 24 h, decant off any water/sediment at the bottom, add tocopherol, label (herb, part, ratio, oil, date).
herb_infused_oil_method.oil_choice: Stable carriers for infusions: olive, HO sunflower, FCO, jojoba, sesame; avoid flax/rosehip/hemp for long infusions.
herb_infused_oil_method.link: Tinctures_Glycerites_Syrups_and_Infused_Oils_and_Butters (same method; this adds the cosmetic angle)

essential_oil_limits.drops_rule: Approx. 20 drops = 1 mL for thin essential oils, but dropper orifice and oil viscosity vary +-30% (vetiver/sandalwood bigger drops). For accuracy weigh: 1% of 100 g = 1 g.
sensitisers: oxidised limonene and linalool hydroperoxides - old/oxidised citrus, lavender, tea tree oils are much more sensitising than fresh; store cold, dark, full
essential_oil_limits.phototoxic: Expressed (cold-pressed) bergamot, lime, lemon, bitter orange, grapefruit (weaker), angelica root, cumin, rue contain furocoumarins (bergapten = 5-MOP). Use distilled or "bergapten-free/FCF" versions in leave-on products for sun-exposed skin, or stay under the limit, or avoid sun/UV for 12-18 h after application.

categories.4: fine fragrance incl. solid perfume, fragrancing cream, non-cream aftershave
categories.12: candles, air fresheners and other non-skin-contact (not intended for skin)

oakmoss extract (and treemoss).spec: atranol and chloroatranol each <100 ppm in the extract

IFRA.additivity_rule: Phototoxic oils are additive: sum of (each oil % / its limit) must not exceed 1 (100%).
IFRA.worked_example: A body lotion (cat 5A) with 0.2% expressed bergamot (half its 0.40% limit) can take at most 1.0% cold-pressed lemon (half of 2.0%).

general_dilution.source: Tisserand Institute general dilution guide (2022) and Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety 2e (2014) children table
general_dilution.children_note: Under 6 the % applies to any topical use; from 6 it is for full-body application and small local areas may be stronger. Avoid menthol (peppermint) and 1,8-cineole oils (eucalyptus, rosemary) on or near the face of infants and young children; EMA: peppermint not under 2, eucalyptus not under 30 months.
general_dilution.pregnancy: No verified Tisserand figure (the commonly repeated "~1%" is NOT his statement). Conservative practice: low dilution, and avoid oils Tisserand & Young contraindicate in pregnancy/breastfeeding (cinnamon bark, cassia, oregano, lemongrass and may chang (citral, teratogenicity), plus the classic abortifacient/emmenagogue oils: pennyroyal, savin, tansy, rue, mugwort, wormwood, thuja, sage (thujone), parsley seed/leaf (apiole), hyssop (pinocamphone), camphor, birch/wintergreen).
general_dilution.drops_math: 1% of 30 mL (~ 27 g oil) = 0.27 g EO ~ 6 drops at ~20 drops/mL; weigh for accuracy.

dermal_maxima.source: Tisserand & Young, Essential Oil Safety 2e (2014), page-cited via Tisserand Institute / AromaWeb reproductions (book text not read directly)

cassia (bark or leaf).reason: cinnamaldehyde sensitisation; also anticoagulant caution, pregnancy contraindicated

oregano.reason: carvacrol sensitisation; pregnancy contraindicated; no topical under 2

lemon (cold-pressed).reason: phototoxicity; distilled lemon not phototoxic; avoid oxidised oil

peppermint.reason: menthol; avoid with cardiac fibrillation, G6PD deficiency; not near infant faces

dermal_maxima.interaction_with_IFRA: Tisserand maxima are per single oil on skin; IFRA limits are per finished product by category and add across oils with the same constituent. Use whichever is lower.

labelling.US: 21 CFR 701.3(a): ingredients in descending order of predominance; "fragrance"/"flavor" may be declared as such. 701.3(f): ingredients >1% in descending order, then <=1% in any order, then colours. MoCRA (signed 29 Dec 2022) adds facility registration, product listing, adverse-event reporting and safety substantiation; FDA was to propose fragrance-allergen labelling by 29 June 2024 - missed; Sept 2025 Unified Agenda targeted a proposed rule for May 2026 (none final as of this compile). Treat/heal claims make a product a drug.
labelling.EU_UK: Responsible person, product information file, safety assessment before sale; INCI list; fragrance allergens named when >0.001% leave-on / >0.01% rinse-off. Reg (EU) 2023/1545 expands the list from ~24-26 to ~80 entries: new products must comply from 31 July 2026, products already on the market by 31 July 2028.
labelling.home_label_minimum: Name, all ingredients by INCI in descending order, date made, batch, "use by" (water-based: 3-6 months if preserved; anhydrous: rancidity-limited, 6-24 months), patch-test instruction, storage, allergens (nut oils!).
labelling.status: verified (21 CFR 701.3; MoCRA status; Reg 2023/1545 dates)

types.dose: 3-5 drops per 100 mL water (manufacturer typical; 100 mL tank ~ 3-5 drops, 300-500 mL ~ 6-15)
types.notes: Clean weekly (biofilm in the tank); use distilled water (tap minerals -> white dust); citrus/oxidised oils degrade plastic.

types.how: Atomises undiluted oil; far higher airborne concentration.
types.dose: run on timers, e.g. 1-5 min on / 10-30 min off; a few mL can go in an hour
types.notes: Most likely to irritate airways, pets, and to form ozone-reaction products. Not for pet or infant rooms.

types.notes: Ingestion hazard for toddlers and pets (spills); flammable bases.

types.type: Passive (clay, wood, inhaler stick, cotton ball)
types.notes: Lowest exposure; personal inhalers 10-20 drops on wick.
Heat oxidises oil; candle burners are a fire risk.

c_diffusers_room_sprays.session_length: Tisserand Institute: diffuse 30-60 minutes on, then 30-60 minutes off; keep some fresh-air exchange; do not directly and intensively inhale for longer than 15-20 minutes. For a child's room, R. Tisserand suggests "2-3 drops over several hours". (verified)

room_spray_recipe.formula: EO 1-3 g (1-3%) premixed with a solubiliser (polysorbate 20 at 2-4x the oil weight, or high-proof ethanol 20-50%), distilled water to 100 g; preservative required if <~20% ethanol (water-based sprays grow microbes)
room_spray_recipe.note: Ethanol-based sprays are flammable; label "shake well" if no solubiliser.

vulnerable_groups.cats: UGT1A6 is a pseudogene in cats: five deleterious exon-1 mutations, no hepatic UGT1A6 mRNA (Court & Greenblatt 2000 Pharmacogenetics 10(4):355-69, PMID 10862526) - poor glucuronidation of phenols and many terpenoid metabolites. Active (ultrasonic/nebulising) diffusers deposit microdroplets on fur that are then groomed off and swallowed (Pet Poison Helpline). ASPCA: cats are especially sensitive; significant ingestion causes GI upset, CNS depression and liver damage; inhaled oil can cause aspiration pneumonia; do not use essential oils where pets have access unless supervised or vet-approved. (verified)
vulnerable_groups.dogs: Khan, McLean, Slater 2014 JAVMA 244(1):95-9: 443 cases (337 dogs, 106 cats) of 100% tea tree oil exposure in ASPCA APCC data 2002-2012; 89% were intentional (owner) use; 0.1-85 mL; signs in 2-12 h lasting up to 72 h - hypersalivation, CNS depression, paresis, ataxia, tremor; small, young cats at greatest risk. (verified)
vulnerable_groups.birds: MSD Veterinary Manual (Toxicoses of Pet Birds): PTFE fumes from nonstick pans overheated to ~280 C often cause acute death; "other aerosols, including some carpet fresheners... perfumes, deodorizers, votive candles... may also be irritating or toxic to caged birds." Do not diffuse, burn candles/incense or spray near birds. (verified)
vulnerable_groups.small_mammals_reptiles: Rabbits, ferrets, rodents and reptiles: small body mass and enclosed cages; avoid.
vulnerable_groups.infants_children: EMA HMPC monographs: peppermint oil must not be used in children under 2 (apnoea/airway constriction listed for inhalation); eucalyptus oil must not be given to children under 30 months (laryngeal spasm) or with a history of seizures. Tisserand & Young: do not apply menthol- or 1,8-cineole-rich oils on or near the face of infants and young children. Ingestion of a few mL of eucalyptus, camphor, wintergreen, clove or tea tree oil is a poisoning emergency in toddlers - store like medicine. (verified)
vulnerable_groups.asthma: Fragrance/VOCs are a common trigger; ultrasonic and nebuliser aerosols deliver particles into airways. If someone in the room has asthma, prefer none, or low-dose passive.
vulnerable_groups.pregnancy: Inhalation at diffuser doses is low exposure; avoid nebulising and the ketone/abortifacient oils.

indoor_air_chemistry.mechanism: Unsaturated terpenes (d-limonene, alpha-pinene, terpinolene, alpha-terpineol, linalool to a lesser degree) react with indoor ozone (from outdoor infiltration, ionisers, "ozone air purifiers", some printers) to form formaldehyde, other aldehydes, hydroxyl radicals and secondary organic aerosol (ultrafine particles). Effect is largest with high ozone (summer, ionisers) and low ventilation.
practical: Never combine an ozone generator/ioniser with diffusers or citrus/pine cleaning
Prefer passive methods in small rooms

pet_avoid_list.source: Pet Poison Helpline (the named list is theirs, not ASPCA's); Texas A&M adds lavender, lemon, lemongrass, rosemary, thyme

waxes.pros: Good cold throw, renewable, soap-and-water cleanup, slow burn
waxes.cons: Frosting, wet spots (glass adhesion), weaker hot throw than paraffin, needs cure

waxes.pros: Best hot throw, smooth, cheap, colour-true
waxes.cons: Fossil; soot claims are mostly about wick/fragrance load/draught, not paraffin per se
waxes.max_fragrance: often 6-12% depending on grade (supplier datasheet; unverified)

waxes.wax: Coconut (hydrogenated coconut, often blended with soy/paraffin/apricot)
waxes.pros: Creamy, excellent glass adhesion, good throw
waxes.cons: Soft; container only; usually a blend

waxes.pros: Long, bright burn, natural honey scent, no fragrance needed
waxes.cons: Poor scent throw, needs larger wicks, cracks/tunnels in containers, expensive; blend with coconut oil 10-20% for containers

fragrance_load.definition: Fragrance load = fragrance weight / wax weight x 100 (some suppliers use total weight). Weigh, do not measure by volume.
fragrance_load.typical: 6-10% of wax weight for most container candles; never exceed the wax manufacturer's maximum (often 10-12%) - excess oil "sweats", weeps, and can make the flame flare.
fragrance_load.essential_oils: Many EOs throw weakly and are expensive at 6-10%; top-note citrus flashes off. EO candles commonly 6-10% but must still meet IFRA category for candles (cat 12 - candles are a low-contact category, but CLP sensitiser labelling still applies to the finished candle).
fragrance_load.supplier_example: CandleScience Golden Brands 464 soy: container max 10% (1.6 oz/lb = 45 g per 454 g); start at 6% (1 oz/lb); tealight 6%. GB 444: 10%. (verified)

flash_point.why: Flash point (closed cup) is the lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to ignite with an ignition source. It is a TRANSPORT/handling flammability index, not the temperature at which fragrance "burns off" in wax. Practical meaning: keep the oil below its flash point while adding (an open pot of hot wax with a low-flash oil near a gas flame is a fire risk); low-flash-point oils (citrus, eucalyptus ~ 45-50 C) evaporate more from the hot pool and give stronger initial hot throw but fade faster. Excess low-flash oil can produce larger flames. Use electric heat, never open flame, and a thermometer.

values_c_closed_cup.note: Supplier SDS/CoA values; vary by lot. Many citrus/conifer oils flash BELOW the 85 C fragrance-add temperature - so add with the pot OFF the heat source, electric heat only, no open flame.

temperature_sequence_soy.add_fragrance: at 185 F (85 C), stir gently ~2 min

wicks.families: Flat braided (CD, ECO - paper-cored or coreless), square braid (beeswax), cored (zinc/cotton/paper), wood. Lead-cored wicks were banned in the US in 2003 (CPSC 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13)).
wicks.sizing: Sized to container diameter and wax; supplier charts are a starting point only. Test 2-3 sizes.
burn_test: Burn 1 h per inch (2.5 cm) of diameter for the first burn so the melt pool reaches the edge (avoids tunnelling memory)
Target melt pool 1/4-1/2 inch (6-13 mm) deep, full diameter within ~2-4 h
Flame 0.5-1.5 inch (1-4 cm), steady, no mushrooming/smoking
Container glass under ~ 60 C (140 F) on the side (common industry target)
Burn to end-of-life: stop at 1/2 inch (13 mm) of wax remaining (ASTM F2417 container end-of-life concept)
Trim wick to 1/4 inch (6 mm) before each burn

d_candles_wax_melts.cure: Soy: at least 48 h before test, 1-2 weeks for full scent throw (crystal structure stabilises); paraffin: 24-72 h; coconut blends: 3-7 days; beeswax: 2-3 days.
d_candles_wax_melts.soot: Soot = incomplete combustion: wick too large or untrimmed (mushrooming), draughts (flicker), too much fragrance, fragrance with many heavy aromatics, or a container that restricts air. Trim wicks, keep out of draughts, cap burns at ~4 h.

wax_melts.what: Scented wax without a wick, warmed in a tealight or electric warmer.
wax_melts.load: 8-12% common (melts tolerate more because they are not burnt)
wax_melts.safety: Tealight warmers are open flames; electric warmers preferred. Wax melts are "mixtures" under EU CLP - CLP hazard labelling (sensitisers, aquatic toxicity) applies like candles.

fire_safety.source: NFPA, Home Candle Fires (M. Ahrens, May 2020; data 2014-2018)
fire_safety.per_year_US: 7,610 home structure fires, 81 civilian deaths, 677 injuries (2% of home fires, 3% of deaths, 6% of injuries; ~21 per day)
fire_safety.causes: 60% - something that could burn was too close; 16% - candle unattended/abandoned; sleep a factor in 10% of fires and 15% of deaths
fire_safety.where_when: bedroom 37% of fires and 40% of deaths; December/January peaks; Christmas ~3x the daily average
rules: Keep candles 12 inches (30 cm) from anything that can burn (NFPA tip sheet)
Never leave burning or fall asleep
Sturdy heat-resistant holder, away from children/pets/draughts
Never use candles near oxygen equipment
Flashlights, not candles, in power cuts

US_ASTM.F2058-07(2021): Standard Specification for Candle Fire Safety Labeling (the pictogram/warning label)
US_ASTM.F2417-26: Standard Specification for Fire Safety for Candles (flame height, secondary ignition, end-of-life, stability)
US_ASTM.F2326-04(2021): Test method for visible soot emissions

labelling.EU_CLP: ECHA guidance ECHA-24-R-06-EN (Aug 2024): candles INCLUDING wax melts are mixtures under REACH/CLP. A fragrance sensitiser at or above 1.0% (Skin Sens. 1B) or 0.1% (1A) makes the candle Skin Sens. 1 (H317); at one tenth of that (0.1% / 0.01%) the label needs EUH208 "Contains [name]. May produce an allergic reaction." A candle with 10% of a fragrance classified as sensitising is itself Skin Sens. 1. Hazard labels go on packaging, not the wax; hazardous candles need a UFI/PCN notification.
labelling.status: ASTM titles and ECHA guidance verified; EN edition years from catalogue snippets

types.stick (masala/charcoal): Bamboo core coated with charcoal/joss (Litsea bark - makko) paste + resins/herbs, or dipped blanks + fragrance
types.loose on charcoal: Resins (frankincense, myrrh, copal, benzoin) on self-lighting charcoal
types.Japanese kodo/senko: Makko-bound wood powders (agarwood, sandalwood) - no charcoal, less smoke
types.heated not burned: Mica plate over charcoal or an electric resin warmer: aroma without combustion smoke

incense.base_ratio: Makko (tabu powder) is the binder and fuel: typical 20-40% makko to 60-80% aromatic powders/resins by weight; mix with warm water to playdough, roll/shape, dry 1-2 weeks slowly (fast drying cracks).
incense.resins: Frankincense (Boswellia), myrrh (Commiphora), copal (Protium/Bursera), benzoin (Styrax), labdanum, dragon's blood (Daemonorops/Dracaena); link: Edible_Waxes_Hive_Foods_and_Aromatic_Resins, Kyphi.
incense.health: Burning incense emits PM2.5, CO, benzene, formaldehyde, PAHs; heavy household incense use is associated in cohort studies with respiratory and some cancer risks (e.g. Singapore Chinese Health Study; not re-verified). Ventilate; never in infant/bird rooms; heated-not-burned methods reduce combustion products.

simmer_pots.method: Water + citrus peel, cinnamon stick, cloves, star anise, rosemary, vanilla, apple, ginger; simmer low on the stove, top up water; discard after 1-2 days (it is a soup, it spoils).
simmer_pots.safety: Never leave unattended or let it boil dry (scorched pot, fire); keep cats away (they may drink it). Uses whole spices - no essential-oil dosing issues.

sachets_potpourri.method: Dried flowers/herbs/spices + fixative (orris root powder, benzoin, oakmoss - note oakmoss is a strong sensitiser - or cellulose/corn-cob granules) + 1-3% essential oil by weight; cure sealed 2-6 weeks shaking occasionally.
sachets_potpourri.moth_herbs: Lavender, cedar, rosemary, southernwood, tansy - repellency is modest; cedar loses activity as it dries out (sand to refresh).
sachets_potpourri.safety: Dried potpourri is harmful if eaten by dogs/children (essential oils, some botanicals). Simmering LIQUID potpourri (often cationic detergents + EOs) is widely reported by veterinary poison services to cause oral/oesophageal burns in cats that lick it - unverified this session (no PubMed record located).

bath_products.bath_salts: Epsom/sea/Dead Sea salt + EO pre-mixed into a dispersant (polysorbate 80 / castile soap / carrier oil); EOs do not dissolve in bathwater and sit neat on the surface - skin irritation and sensitisation happen this way.
bath_products.bath_bombs: Baking soda : citric acid ~2:1 by weight, + 10-20% cornstarch/clay, binder spritz (witch hazel/alcohol), 1-2% fragrance, optional SLSa/polysorbate; humidity sets them off - pack dry.
bath_products.bath_oils: Dispersing bath oil = carrier + 10-20% polysorbate 80 (or Turkey red oil, sulfated castor) so the oil disperses instead of slicking the tub (slip hazard).
bath_products.scrubs: Sugar/salt + oil 2:1; emulsified scrubs (with emulsifier) rinse clean; if used in a wet shower, water gets in - preserve or use small jars.

soap_brief.link: Soap_Calculator (our tool) - use it for every batch; this is only the safety frame.
lye_safety: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) for bars, potassium hydroxide (KOH) for liquid/soft soap; both cause deep alkaline burns and blindness
Goggles (not glasses) + nitrile gloves + long sleeves; ventilate (dissolving NaOH releases heat ~ to 80-90 C and caustic mist)
Always add LYE to WATER, never water to lye (eruption); use heat-proof stainless steel or PP #5 plastic - never aluminium (reacts, hydrogen gas) or tin
Keep vinegar for surfaces only - for skin and eyes flush with running water for 15+ minutes and seek care; do not "neutralise" a burn with acid
soap_brief.superfat: Lye discount 5-8% for bars (excess oil, milder); 0-3% for liquid soap (excess oil clouds/goes rancid); 15-20% for 100% coconut "salt bar"-style recipes.
soap_brief.water: Lye concentration 25-40% (water:lye 1.5:1 to 3:1). Higher water = slower trace, longer cure, more soda ash.
soap_brief.cure: Cold process 4-6 weeks (water evaporation, crystal structure), castile 3-12 months.
soap_brief.zap_test_and_pH: Finished CP soap pH ~9-10.5 is normal (soap is the salt of a weak acid); pH > ~11 or a "zap" (tongue tingle test - not recommended; use phenolphthalein drops instead: pink = alkaline but all soap turns faintly pink) suggests excess lye - rebatch.
soap_brief.conflict_flag: Our soapcalc.mjs palm kernel SAP (0.156 NaOH) is below Codex/SoapCalc range (0.164-0.181; SoapCalc 0.176) - see NOTES.md.

how_to_read.direction: raises/lowers = exposure (blood level, AUC) of the named drug, unless stated as additive effect
how_to_read.significance: major = avoid or needs monitoring/dose change; moderate = clinically noticeable in some people; minor/theoretical = mostly lab or single-case
how_to_read.evidence: clinical trial > case series > case report > animal > in vitro. In vitro CYP inhibition frequently fails to translate in people (kava, pomegranate, cranberry, kratom 2D6, goldenseal-metformin).

core_mechanisms.CYP3A4 inhibition (gut, irreversible): grapefruit/Seville orange/pomelo furanocoumarins; effect lasts 24-72 h, so spacing doses does not help
core_mechanisms.CYP3A4/P-gp induction (PXR): St John's wort (hyperforin), garlic supplements for saquinavir; onset over days, offset ~2 weeks
core_mechanisms.CYP1A2 induction: smoke (tobacco or cannabis PAHs), charbroiled meat, cruciferous veg; stopping smoking RAISES clozapine/olanzapine
core_mechanisms.CYP1A2 inhibition: fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin raise caffeine; caffeine competes with clozapine
core_mechanisms.MAO-A inhibition: tyramine pressor crisis (irreversible MAOIs strongly; RIMA/harmala less but dose-dependent), serotonin toxicity with serotonergics
core_mechanisms.Additive CNS depression: alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, kava, valerian, gabapentinoids
core_mechanisms.Mineralocorticoid excess: licorice glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits 11beta-HSD2 -> hypokalaemia, hypertension; dangerous with thiazide/loop diuretics, digoxin, QT drugs
core_mechanisms.Vitamin K / platelets: greens (consistency matters), ginkgo/garlic (weak, mostly case reports), topical methyl salicylate with warfarin (real)

interactions.mechanism: Mechanism-based (irreversible) inactivation of intestinal (enterocyte) CYP3A4 by furanocoumarins; hepatic CYP3A4 largely spared. Effect lasts ~24-72 h until new enzyme is synthesized.
interactions.direction: Raises felodipine exposure (mean bioavailability 284% of water, range 164-469%); lower diastolic BP, higher heart rate. Nifedipine only 134%.

sources.citation: Bailey DG et al. Interaction of citrus juices with felodipine and nifedipine. Lancet 1991
Bailey DG et al. Grapefruit-medication interactions: forbidden fruit or avoidable consequences? CMAJ 2013

interactions.notes: One glass can be enough; spacing doses does not reliably avoid it because the enzyme is destroyed, not just competitively blocked.

interactions.mechanism: Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation; simvastatin/lovastatin have very high first-pass CYP3A4 extraction, so the effect is large.
interactions.direction: Raises statin and active acid exposure: double-strength juice 200 mL tid -> simvastatin Cmax ~9-fold, AUC far higher; lovastatin ~15-fold; one ordinary 200 mL glass daily for 3 days -> simvastatin AUC ~3.6-fold. Atorvastatin moderately raised; pravastatin unaffected.

sources.citation: Lilja JJ et al. Grapefruit juice-simvastatin interaction. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1998
Kantola T et al. Grapefruit juice greatly increases serum concentrations of lovastatin and lovastatin acid. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1998
Lilja JJ et al. Effects of regular consumption of grapefruit juice on the pharmacokinetics of simvastatin. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2004

interactions.notes: Risk is dose-related myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. Pravastatin/rosuvastatin are the non-CYP3A4 alternatives (Lilja 1999, PMID 10460065).

interactions.mechanism: Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation; only the oral route is affected.
interactions.direction: Raises oral midazolam AUC ~52%, Cmax ~56%, stronger sedation; IV midazolam unchanged. Raises triazolam concentrations (~48% AUC).

sources.citation: Kupferschmidt HH et al. Interaction between grapefruit juice and midazolam in humans. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1995
Hukkinen SK et al. Plasma concentrations of triazolam are increased by concomitant ingestion of grapefruit juice. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1995

interactions.notes: IV-unchanged result is the textbook proof that the site is the gut wall, not the liver.

interactions.mechanism: Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation plus possible intestinal P-gp effects.
interactions.direction: Raises oral cyclosporine AUC (~55%) and Cmax (~35%); IV cyclosporine unaffected.

sources.citation: Ducharme MP et al. Disposition of intravenous and oral cyclosporine after administration with grapefruit juice. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1995
Yee GC et al. Effect of grapefruit juice on blood cyclosporin concentration. Lancet 1995
Edwards DJ et al. 6',7'-Dihydroxybergamottin in grapefruit juice and Seville orange juice: effects on cyclosporine disposition, enterocyte CYP3A4, and P-glycoprotein. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1999

interactions.notes: Historically some transplant centres used it deliberately as a 'cyclosporine-sparing' agent; abandoned because juice furanocoumarin content varies batch to batch.

interactions.mechanism: Same furanocoumarins (bergamottin, 6',7'-DHB) inactivate intestinal CYP3A4; pomelo also inhibits P-gp in vitro.
interactions.direction: Seville orange raised felodipine AUC 76% (grapefruit 93% in same study). Pomelo raised cyclosporine AUC/Cmax (~19%/12%) and caused a clinically significant tacrolimus rise in a renal transplant case. Sweet (common) orange juice has no effect.
interactions.evidence: clinical trials + case report + in vitro

sources.citation: Malhotra S et al. Seville orange juice-felodipine interaction: comparison with dilute grapefruit juice and involvement of furocoumarins. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2001
Grenier J et al. Pomelo juice, but not cranberry juice, affects the pharmacokinetics of cyclosporine in humans. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2006
Egashira K et al. Pomelo-induced increase in the blood level of tacrolimus in a renal transplant patient. Transplantation 2003

interactions.notes: CORRECTION/nuance: Edwards 1999 (PMID 10096255) found Seville orange juice cut enterocyte CYP3A4 by ~40% yet did NOT change cyclosporine disposition, whereas grapefruit raised it 55% - so the cyclosporine effect of grapefruit is not explained by furanocoumarin CYP3A4 loss alone (P-gp/other constituents implicated). 'All bitter citrus = grapefruit for every drug' is an oversimplification. Limes and some tangelos also contain furanocoumarins.

interactions.mechanism: Hyperforin activates PXR -> induction of intestinal/hepatic CYP3A4 and intestinal P-gp (MDR1).
interactions.direction: Lowers cyclosporine levels (profound trough drops); acute rejection reported.

sources.citation: Ruschitzka F et al. Acute heart transplant rejection due to Saint John's wort. Lancet 2000
Breidenbach T et al. Profound drop of cyclosporin A whole blood trough levels caused by St. John's wort. Transplantation 2000
Durr D et al. St John's Wort induces intestinal P-glycoprotein/MDR1 and intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2000

interactions.notes: Induction takes ~1-2 weeks to develop and ~2 weeks to wear off; stopping SJW abruptly can push cyclosporine into toxic range. Low-hyperforin extracts have much weaker effects.

interactions.mechanism: CYP3A4 induction (PXR) increases clearance of both estrogen and progestin.
interactions.direction: Lowers contraceptive exposure: increased norethindrone oral clearance, shorter ethinyl estradiol half-life; increased breakthrough bleeding and evidence of follicle growth/ovulation.

sources.citation: Hall SD et al. The interaction between St John's wort and an oral contraceptive. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2003

Murphy PA et al. Interaction of St. John's Wort with oral contraceptives: effects on the pharmacokinetics of norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol, ovarian activity and breakthrough bleeding. Contraception 2005

interactions.notes: Use backup contraception during and for ~2 weeks after SJW.

interactions.mechanism: CYP3A4 (+P-gp) induction.
interactions.direction: Lowers indinavir AUC ~57% and trough ~81% in healthy volunteers - risk of HIV treatment failure and resistance.

sources.citation: Piscitelli SC et al. Indinavir concentrations and St John's wort. Lancet 2000

interactions.notes: Percentages from the Lancet letter as widely reported; title/author/year confirmed. Surprising contrast: Burstein 2000 (PMID 11180020) found no SJW effect on carbamazepine, attributed to carbamazepine already maximally auto-inducing CYP3A4.

interactions.mechanism: Induction of intestinal P-glycoprotein (MDR1) -> reduced absorption (digoxin is a P-gp probe, not CYP-metabolized).
interactions.direction: Lowers digoxin AUC ~25% and troughs ~33% after 10 days.
interactions.significance: moderate (major for patients dependent on tight digoxin levels)

sources.citation: Johne A et al. Pharmacokinetic interaction of digoxin with an herbal extract from St John's wort. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1999
Durr D et al. St John's Wort induces intestinal P-glycoprotein/MDR1 and intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2000

interactions.notes: Shows SJW is a transporter inducer, not only a CYP inducer - affects P-gp substrates (dabigatran, fexofenadine, some chemotherapy).

agents: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine), nefazodone, other serotonergic drugs
interactions.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic: hyperforin inhibits reuptake of serotonin (and other monoamines) -> additive serotonergic activity.
interactions.direction: Additive effect -> serotonin syndrome (agitation, tremor, clonus, hyperthermia).

sources.citation: Lantz MS et al. St. John's wort and antidepressant drug interactions in the elderly. J Geriatr Psychiatry Neurol 1999
Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. N Engl J Med 2005

interactions.notes: Evidence is case-level only; SJW also lowers levels of many antidepressants via induction (e.g. amitriptyline, Johne 2002 PMID 11799342) - two opposite risks at once.

interactions.mechanism: Induction of CYP2C9 (S-warfarin) and CYP3A4/1A2 (R-warfarin).
interactions.direction: Lowers warfarin exposure: S-warfarin clearance rose from ~198 to ~270 mL/h; reduced INR / anticoagulant effect. Swedish reports of falling INR.
interactions.significance: major (loss of anticoagulation; bleeding when SJW is stopped)

sources.citation: Jiang X et al. Effect of St John's wort and ginseng on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of warfarin in healthy subjects. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2004
Yue QY et al. Safety of St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum). Lancet 2000

interactions.notes: Direction is the reverse of the common 'herbs make you bleed' intuition: SJW makes warfarin weaker.

interactions.mechanism: Inhibition (partly mechanism-based, methylenedioxyphenyl alkaloids) of CYP2D6 and CYP3A4/5.
interactions.direction: Raises exposure of CYP2D6 substrates (debrisoquine ratio ~40% inhibition) and CYP3A substrates (midazolam ~40% inhibition; midazolam AUC up in later studies).

sources.citation: Gurley BJ et al. In vivo effects of goldenseal, kava kava, black cohosh, and valerian on human cytochrome P450 1A2, 2D6, 2E1, and 3A4/5 phenotypes. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2005
Gurley BJ et al. Clinical assessment of CYP2D6-mediated herb-drug interactions in humans. Mol Nutr Food Res 2008
Gurley BJ et al. Supplementation with goldenseal, but not kava kava, inhibits human CYP3A activity in vivo. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2008

interactions.notes: Goldenseal was the only one of the four botanicals in Gurley 2005 to inhibit both 2D6 and 3A4 meaningfully.

interactions.mechanism: Predicted from in vitro: inhibition of OCT1/2 and MATE1/2-K transporters. Observed in vivo: reduced absorption, mechanism not fully explained (possibly intestinal uptake/OCT3 or other).
interactions.direction: LOWERS metformin AUC (GMR ~0.77) and Cmax (~0.73); no change in half-life or renal clearance. Midazolam (CYP3A) AUC raised as positive control; no effect on rosuvastatin or furosemide.
interactions.evidence: clinical trial (16 healthy volunteers, probe cocktail)

sources.citation: Nguyen JT et al. Assessing Transporter-Mediated Natural Product-Drug Interactions Via In vitro-In Vivo Extrapolation: Clinical Evaluation With a Probe Cocktail. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2021

interactions.notes: CORRECTION: the expected direction from in vitro OCT/MATE inhibition (higher metformin) was wrong in vivo - metformin exposure went DOWN. Note berberine itself lowers glucose, adding a pharmacodynamic element.

agents: tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured/fermented meats, tap beer, soy/fermented products, spoiled food)
interactions.mechanism: Inhibition of gut/liver MAO-A removes first-pass metabolism of dietary tyramine; tyramine displaces noradrenaline from nerve terminals -> pressor response.
interactions.direction: Additive/pressor effect: hypertensive crisis (occipital headache, stroke risk).
interactions.significance: major for irreversible non-selective MAOIs; much less for RIMAs (moclobemide) and transdermal low-dose selegiline
interactions.evidence: clinical case series + human pressor-challenge data + animal

sources.citation: Blackwell B. Tyramine in cheese related to hypertensive crises after monoamine-oxidase inhibition. Lancet 1965
Blackwell B et al. Hypertensive interactions between monoamine oxidase inhibitors and foodstuffs. Br J Psychiatry 1967
Gillman PK. A reassessment of the safety profile of monoamine oxidase inhibitors: elucidating tired old tyramine myths. J Neural Transm 2018

interactions.notes: CORRECTION: older 'avoid everything' lists (chocolate, bananas, avocado, coffee, wine in general) are mostly overcautious; Gillman 2018 and Van den Eynde 2022 (PMID 35721816) note modern commercial cheeses mostly have low tyramine and the real hazards are aged/artisanal cheese, tap/unpasteurised beer, fermented soy, cured sausage and spoiled/long-stored protein foods. Threshold for a significant pressor response is roughly a few tens of mg tyramine per sitting on irreversible MAOIs (~6-10 mg can produce measurable effects; >=25 mg dangerous).

agents: SSRIs / SNRIs / clomipramine / tramadol / meperidine (pethidine) / dextromethorphan / methadone / tapentadol
interactions.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic: MAO inhibition + serotonin reuptake inhibition -> massive synaptic serotonin (5-HT2A/1A over-stimulation).
interactions.direction: Additive/synergistic -> severe serotonin toxicity (hyperthermia, clonus, rigidity, death).
interactions.significance: major (contraindicated; washout required - 2 weeks after MAOI; 5 weeks after fluoxetine)

sources.citation: Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. N Engl J Med 2005
Gillman PK. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors, opioid analgesics and serotonin toxicity. Br J Anaesth 2005

interactions.notes: Gillman: only opioids that are serotonin reuptake inhibitors (meperidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan, dextropropoxyphene, tapentadol) carry this risk; morphine, oxycodone, codeine, buprenorphine do not. Meperidine+MAOI also has a separate 'excitatory' reaction history.

agents: harmala alkaloids (harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine; Peganum harmala seeds, Banisteriopsis caapi/ayahuasca)
SSRIs and other serotonin reuptake inhibitors
interactions.mechanism: Harmine/harmaline are potent reversible MAO-A inhibitors (RIMA-like); THH also weakly inhibits serotonin reuptake. Combined with an SSRI -> serotonin toxicity mechanism as for MAOI+SSRI; DMT in ayahuasca adds 5-HT2A agonism.
interactions.direction: Additive/synergistic serotonergic effect -> serotonin syndrome.
interactions.evidence: case reports + human PK of ayahuasca alkaloids

sources.citation: Callaway JC, Grob CS. Ayahuasca preparations and serotonin reuptake inhibitors: a potential combination for severe adverse interactions. J Psychoactive Drugs 1998
Callaway JC et al. Pharmacokinetics of Hoasca alkaloids in healthy humans. J Ethnopharmacol 1999
Malcolm BJ, Lee KC. Ayahuasca: An ancient sacrament for treatment of contemporary psychiatric illness? Ment Health Clin 2017

interactions.notes: Common retreat guidance: stop SSRIs with a prescriber-supervised taper and washout (fluoxetine ~5-6 weeks) - abrupt SSRI discontinuation has its own risks. Peganum harmala seeds are a more concentrated harmala source than caapi; P. harmala poisoning cases exist independent of SSRIs (e.g. PMID 24955262).

interactions.mechanism: Reversible competitive MAO-A inhibition; high tyramine concentrations can partly displace a reversible inhibitor, so pressor potentiation is smaller than with irreversible MAOIs but not zero, and largest during peak harmine levels (first few hours).
interactions.direction: Additive pressor effect (raised tyramine exposure) -> possible hypertensive reaction.
interactions.evidence: in vitro + pharmacological extrapolation from RIMAs; no controlled human tyramine challenge with harmala found

sources.citation: Berlowitz I et al. Monoamine Oxidase Inhibition by Plant-Derived beta-Carbolines; Implications for the Psychopharmacology of Tobacco and Ayahuasca. Front Pharmacol 2022
Gillman PK. A reassessment of the safety profile of monoamine oxidase inhibitors: elucidating tired old tyramine myths. J Neural Transm 2018

interactions.notes: Traditional 'dieta' food restrictions overlap with but are not identical to MAOI tyramine lists. Harmine half-life is short (hours), so risk window is the day of the ceremony rather than weeks.

agents: harmala alkaloids / ayahuasca (or any MAO-A inhibitor)
interactions.mechanism: MAO-A inhibition prevents breakdown of serotonin/noradrenaline released by MDMA/amphetamines -> massive monoamine excess.
interactions.direction: Synergistic -> serotonin toxicity, hyperthermia, hypertensive crisis; fatalities with MDMA + moclobemide.
interactions.evidence: forensic case reports (with moclobemide, a pharmacological analog of harmala) + animal microdialysis; no harmala-specific clinical study

sources.citation: Vuori E et al. Death following ingestion of MDMA (ecstasy) and moclobemide. Addiction 2003
Pilgrim JL et al. Serotonin toxicity involving MDMA (ecstasy) and moclobemide. Forensic Sci Int 2012
Freezer A et al. Effects of MDMA and para-methoxyamphetamine on striatal 5-HT when co-administered with moclobemide. Brain Res 2005

interactions.notes: Evidence for harmala specifically is by mechanistic analogy (harmine is a reversible MAO-A inhibitor like moclobemide but more potent). PMA/PMMA (often sold as 'ecstasy') are themselves MAO-A inhibitors and especially dangerous here.

interactions.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic additive CNS depression (kavalactones modulate GABA-A, block Na+/Ca2+ channels); possible additive hepatic stress.
interactions.direction: Additive: kava alone had little effect but kava + alcohol produced greater impairment on divided attention and subjective intoxication than alcohol alone.

sources.citation: Foo H, Lemon J. Acute effects of kava, alone or in combination with alcohol, on subjective measures of impairment and intoxication and on cognitive performance. Drug Alcohol Rev 1997
Herberg KW. Effect of Kava-Special Extract WS 1490 combined with ethyl alcohol on safety-relevant performance parameters. Blutalkohol 1993

interactions.notes: Herberg 1993 (standardized pharmaceutical extract, lower dose) found no potentiation - results depend on dose and preparation (traditional beverage vs extract).

interactions.mechanism: Idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; proposed contributors: poor-quality raw material (aerial parts/peelings containing pipermethystine, mould/aflatoxin), acetone/ethanol extracts vs water extracts, kavalactone CYP inhibition with co-medications, CYP2D6 poor-metabolizer status.
interactions.direction: Adverse effect (hepatitis, rare liver failure/transplant).
interactions.evidence: case series + causality assessments (RUCAM/WHO) + regulatory reviews

sources.citation: Teschke R. Kava hepatotoxicity--a clinical review. Ann Hepatol 2010
Stickel F et al. Hepatitis induced by Kava (Piper methysticum rhizoma). J Hepatol 2003
WHO. Assessment of the risk of hepatotoxicity with kava products. Geneva: World Health Organization, 2007 (not indexed in PubMed; not fetched)

interactions.notes: Debate: many of the ~100 European reports had weak causality on re-assessment (Teschke), and Germany's 2002 ban was overturned by court in 2014. WHO 2007 concluded risk is real but low and recommended water-based extracts of peeled rhizome/root of 'noble' cultivars. Avoid with alcohol, other hepatotoxins, and pre-existing liver disease.
interactions.type: toxicity (agent alone or with liver/CNS load)

interactions.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic additive GABAergic CNS depression; possible additional PK contribution (kavalactone CYP inhibition) not established.
interactions.direction: Additive sedation -> lethargic, disoriented semi-comatose state.

sources.citation: Almeida JC, Grimsley EW. Coma from the health food store: interaction between kava and alprazolam. Ann Intern Med 1996

interactions.notes: CORRECTION: the patient was 'semi-comatose'/lethargic, not in deep coma despite the title, and was also taking cimetidine and terazosin - confounded single case.

agents: CYP2E1 substrates (chlorzoxazone probe; also ethanol, acetaminophen metabolism)
interactions.mechanism: Inhibition of CYP2E1.
interactions.direction: Raises CYP2E1 substrate exposure (~40% reduction in chlorzoxazone 6-hydroxylation ratio). Kava did NOT inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2D6 or CYP3A in vivo in Gurley's studies.

sources.citation: Gurley BJ et al. In vivo effects of goldenseal, kava kava, black cohosh, and valerian on human cytochrome P450 1A2, 2D6, 2E1, and 3A4/5 phenotypes. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2005
Gurley BJ et al. Supplementation with goldenseal, but not kava kava, inhibits human CYP3A activity in vivo. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2008

interactions.notes: CORRECTION: in vitro claims that kava strongly inhibits CYP3A4/2D6 did not hold up clinically; the in vivo signal is CYP2E1.

interactions.mechanism: Myristicin/elemicin: anticholinergic-like and psychoactive effects; myristicin is a weak MAO inhibitor in vitro and is metabolised (CYP) to amphetamine-like derivatives (debated).
interactions.direction: Toxic effect: tachycardia, agitation, hallucinations, nausea, dry mouth, prolonged (24-48 h) intoxication.

sources.citation: Ehrenpreis JE et al. Nutmeg poisonings: a retrospective review of 10 years experience from the Illinois Poison Center, 2001-2011. J Med Toxicol 2014

interactions.notes: Ehrenpreis: many unintentional exposures were in children under 13; intentional exposures were mostly adolescents/young adults seeking a high. Onset is delayed (3-8 h), prompting dangerous redosing. Weak MAO inhibition -> theoretical caution with serotonergics.
interactions.type: toxicity (agent alone or with liver/CNS load)

interactions.mechanism: Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits renal 11beta-HSD2 -> cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors (apparent mineralocorticoid excess/pseudohyperaldosteronism).
interactions.direction: Additive potassium loss with K-wasting diuretics -> hypokalaemia, hypertension, metabolic alkalosis, rhabdomyolysis/paralysis, arrhythmia; also antagonises antihypertensives/spironolactone-sparing effect.
interactions.evidence: mechanistic human studies + many case reports

sources.citation: Stewart PM et al. Mineralocorticoid activity of liquorice: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency comes of age. Lancet 1987
Ferrari P et al. In vivo 11beta-HSD-2 activity: variability, salt-sensitivity, and effect of licorice. Hypertension 2001
Yasue H et al. Severe hypokalemia, rhabdomyolysis, muscle paralysis, and respiratory impairment in a hypertensive patient taking herbal medicines containing licorice. Intern Med 2007

interactions.notes: Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) and most 'licorice'-flavoured anise candy lack this effect. Effects can persist ~1-2 weeks after stopping.

interactions.mechanism: Indirect pharmacodynamic: licorice-induced hypokalaemia increases myocardial sensitivity to digoxin (enhanced Na+/K+-ATPase binding).
interactions.direction: Additive -> digoxin toxicity (arrhythmia) at otherwise 'therapeutic' digoxin levels.
interactions.significance: major (theoretically strong; documented by case report)
interactions.evidence: case report (Harada et al. 2002, Japanese elderly patient - not confirmed in PubMed by this search) + well-established hypokalaemia-digoxin pharmacology

sources.citation: Harada T et al. Congestive heart failure caused by digitalis toxicity in an elderly man taking a licorice-containing Chinese herbal laxative. Cardiology 2002 (PMID not confirmed by search)
Stewart PM et al. Mineralocorticoid activity of liquorice: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency comes of age. Lancet 1987

interactions.notes: No direct PK interaction; the danger is entirely via potassium. Risk compounded when a loop/thiazide diuretic is also used.

interactions.mechanism: Proposed: ginkgolide B platelet-activating-factor antagonism (antiplatelet); no meaningful CYP2C9 effect.
interactions.direction: Controlled data: NO change in INR or S/R-warfarin PK, and no warfarin dose change needed in an RCT. Case reports: spontaneous bleeding (hyphema, subdural haematoma) - additive antiplatelet effect not consistently reproduced.
interactions.significance: minor-to-moderate (case-report signal not confirmed by trials)
interactions.evidence: RCTs + PK/PD study (negative) vs case reports (positive)

sources.citation: Jiang X et al. Effect of ginkgo and ginger on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of warfarin in healthy subjects. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2005
Engelsen J et al. Effect of coenzyme Q10 and Ginkgo biloba on warfarin dosage in stable, long-term warfarin treated outpatients. Thromb Haemost 2002
